source_text: Πάσης ἀγαθῆς ἡ καταρχὴ πράξεως ἐν τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ βουλῇ τὴν ὑπόστασιν κέκτηται, τὸ δὲ συμπέρασμα ἐν τῷ θεῷ.
thought_title: Beginning in human will, completion in God
orientation: Methodius is closing the treatise by stating the principle that grounds his argument about martyrdom as a divine gift.
pass_a_gloss: Of every good action the beginning has acquired its substance in our will, but the completion is in God.

choices.why: Glossary term; renders the starting point of an action.
Glossary term; human intention or resolve.
Glossary term; the grounding reality of the beginning in human will.
Glossary term; the conclusion or fulfillment of the action.
Perfect tense of κτάομαι; conveys a state of possession resulting from acquisition.

pass_b_english: Every good action has its beginning in our will, in which it has its substance, but its completion rests with God.

problems.why: κέκτηται means 'has/possesses,' not 'acquires'; ὑπόστασις is 'substance' but the clause structure is misrendered.
problems.fix: Every good action has its beginning in our will, in which it has its substance, but its completion rests with God.
problems.ruling: κέκτηται is perfect 'has/possesses,' not 'acquires'; misrendered as process. Also 'where' wrongly makes βουλῇ locative rather than source.

edits.new: in which it has its substance

fixed: Changed 'where it acquires its substance' to 'in which it has its substance' because κέκτηται means 'has/possesses,' not 'acquires,' and the relative clause should reflect possession rather than acquisition.

last_rejected.quote: in which it has its substance
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐν τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ βουλῇ τὴν ὑπόστασιν κέκτηται
last_rejected.why: Relative 'which' wrongly refers to 'will' not 'beginning'; 'substance' belongs to the beginning, not will.
last_rejected.fix: Every good action has its beginning in our will, and this beginning has its substance there, but its completion rests with God.
last_rejected.ruling: Greek syntax: ἐν τῇ βουλῇ τὴν ὑπόστασιν κέκτηται means 'in our will it has substance'; 'which' correctly refers to will, not beginning.
